faq.a: When hepatocytes are exhausted, they no longer release enzymes, so ALT may fall despite worsening function.
faq.q: Why can ALT be normal in severe liver disease?

faq.a: Urine dipstick for protein, glucose and ketones gives rapid clues to renal, metabolic and diabetic status.
faq.q: What is the most useful bedside test when labs are unavailable?

faq.a: Severe malaria causes hemolysis (high LDH, indirect bilirubin), renal impairment (raised creatinine) and metabolic acidosis (low HCO3-).
faq.q: How does malaria affect blood biochemistry?

exam: A 28‑year‑old with falciparum malaria presents with confusion; creatinine is 2.2 mg/dL – what is the next immediate step? — Assess fluid status, correct hypovolaemia, and consider urgent dialysis if oliguria persists.

A patient on herbal remedies has ALT 350 U/L, ALP 120 U/L – how do you differentiate drug‑induced hepatitis from cholestasis? — Look for disproportionate ALT rise, check bilirubin pattern, and ask about recent herb use.
Why is serum potassium >6.0 mmol/L an emergency even if the patient feels well? — High potassium can cause fatal arrhythmias; treatment must start before ECG changes appear.

In a child with sickle cell disease, a sudden rise in bilirubin to 12 mg/dL occurs; what causes must be ruled out first? — Acute hemolysis vs hepatic sequestration; check LDH, haptoglobin and ultrasound.

How would you interpret a normal creatinine in a severely malnourished patient with suspected renal failure? — Recognise that low muscle mass can mask renal dysfunction; rely on urine output and urea.

A patient with HIV presents with mild ALT elevation (80 U/L) and high ALP (300 U/L); what is the most likely process? — Cholestatic pattern suggests HIV‑related cholangiopathy or opportunistic infection.
When is it appropriate to forgo a lactate measurement in sepsis? — If lactate is unavailable, use clinical perfusion markers (capillary refill, mental status, urine output) to guide resuscitation.
What electrolyte abnormality is most likely to cause seizures in a patient with severe diarrhoea? — Hyponatraemia (<125 mmol/L) from fluid loss; correct slowly to avoid osmotic demyelination.
ai.title: Blood Biochemistry in Clinical Practice
ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Blood biochemistry provides vital clues to organ function, metabolic disorders and acute illness. Understanding test interpretation, limitations and common tropical causes guides bedside decisions in low‑resource settings.

b: Core panel: Na+, K+, Cl-, HCO3-, glucose, urea, creatinine, ALT, AST, ALP, total bilirubin, albumin.
Interpretation links lab values to pathophysiology, not just normal/abnormal lists.
sections.p: Blood biochemistry measures metabolites, enzymes and electrolytes that reflect cellular activity, organ perfusion and systemic disease. In East African hospitals the core panel often includes glucose, electrolytes, renal function, liver enzymes, bilirubin and a few disease‑specific markers.

b: ALT/AST rise → hepatocellular injury; ALP rise → cholestasis or bone disease.
Creatinine rise → reduced glomerular filtration; urea rise may reflect catabolism or dehydration.
sections.p: Enzymes leak from damaged cells, metabolites accumulate when clearance fails, and electrolytes shift with fluid balance. The laboratory uses spectrophotometry, enzymatic assays and ion‑selective electrodes to generate quantitative results.

b: ADH and aldosterone regulate Na+ and water balance; failure leads to hyponatremia or hypernatremia.
Insulin drives glucose into cells; insulin deficiency or resistance causes hyperglycaemia.
sections.p: Homeostatic mechanisms (renal excretion, hepatic metabolism, hormonal control) keep serum values within narrow ranges. Disruption by infection, drugs or organ failure produces characteristic patterns.

b: Malaria severe anemia → low Hb, high LDH, indirect bilirubin.
HIV‑related nephropathy → rising creatinine, proteinuria, low albumin.
Schistosomiasis hepatic fibrosis → raised ALP, γ‑GT, modest ALT/AST.
Herbal hepatotoxins → disproportionate ALT/AST rise with normal ALP.
sections.p: Common tropical and low‑resource problems produce distinct biochemical signatures.

b: Acute kidney injury: creatinine rise ≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 h or ≥1.5× baseline → urgent fluid assessment.
Severe malaria: lactate >2 mmol/L or creatinine >1.5 mg/dL → consider exchange transfusion or dialysis.
Hepatic failure: INR >1.5 with bilirubin >5 mg/dL → high mortality, need for transfer.
sections.p: Interpretation guides immediate management, prognostication and monitoring of therapy. Recognising patterns avoids misdiagnosis and directs limited resources to the most urgent need.

t.b: Assess fluid‑electrolyte balance; guide IV therapy. Low Na+ (<130 mmol/L) suggests hyponatraemia from SIADH or volume overload.
Detect acute kidney injury and guide drug dosing. Creatinine ≥1.5 mg/dL in a young adult signals impaired GFR.
Differentiate hepatocellular vs cholestatic injury. ALT >5× ULN with normal ALP → viral hepatitis; ALP >2× ULN with modest ALT → cholestasis or schistosomiasis.
Screen for diabetes or stress hyperglycaemia. Random glucose ≥200 mg/dL with symptoms → diabetes.
Identify tissue hypoxia in severe malaria or sepsis. Lactate >2 mmol/L indicates poor perfusion.

b: Acute kidney injury: optimise volume status, avoid nephrotoxins, consider dialysis if creatinine >3 mg/dL or oliguria <0.5 mL/kg/h.
Hyperkalaemia (>5.5 mmol/L): give calcium gluconate (if available), insulin‑glucose, and consider exchange transfusion in severe malaria.
Severe hyperbilirubinaemia (>10 mg/dL) in malaria: treat parasite load, consider phototherapy or exchange transfusion if risk of kernicterus.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then correct the biochemical derangement.

b: Elevated AST in muscle injury vs liver disease – check CK levels if possible.
Hypernatremia from dehydration vs hyperglycaemia‑induced osmotic shift – measure glucose.
Low ALT in advanced cirrhosis despite severe liver damage.
Normal creatinine in early renal failure when muscle mass is low (common in malnourished patients).
Always correlate a single abnormal value with clinical picture; isolated mild ALT rise is often benign.
In low‑resource settings, prioritize tests that change immediate management (e.g., glucose, electrolytes, creatinine).

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden rise in creatinine >2 mg/dL with oliguria
Serum potassium >6.0 mmol/L with ECG changes
Glucose <40 mg/dL with seizures or loss of consciousness
